Fit an edge mixture model

Source: R/bison_mixture.R
bison_mixture.Rd

Looks for clusters (components) in the edge weights, which can be interpreted as different types of social relationship, such as weak and strong bonds. Use it after bison_model() to ask whether the network contains distinct types of edge, and which edges belong to each type.

Usage

bison_mixture(
  edgemodel,
  num_components = 5,
  criterion = c("ICL", "BIC"),
  verbose = TRUE,
  num_draws = 200
)

Arguments

edgemodel

A fitted bison_model object.

num_components

Maximum number of components to consider.

criterion

"ICL" (default) or "BIC": the information criterion used to weigh the different numbers of components. BIC (Bayesian information criterion) measures how well the mixture fits the edge weights. ICL (integrated completed likelihood) also penalises components that overlap, so it favours clearly separated clusters.

verbose

Whether to show a progress bar.

num_draws

Number of posterior draws to fit mixtures to (at most the number available). More draws give more precise probabilities but take longer.

Value

A bison_mixture object. Use summary() on it for an overview, get_network_component_probabilities() for the probability of each number of components, get_edge_component_probabilities() for the component of each edge, get_component_means() for the component means, and plot_mixture() to plot them. Its draw_ids element gives the rows of edgemodel$edge_samples used for each mixture draw, so component assignments can be matched to the edge weights of the same draw.

Details

A Gaussian mixture model describes the edge weights as coming from several normal distributions (the components), each with its own mean and spread. It is fitted with the mclust package to the edge weights (on the link scale) in each of num_draws posterior draws, for every number of components from 1 to num_components. In each draw, the numbers of components are weighted by an information criterion, a measure of fit that penalises complexity. Averaging over draws gives the probability of each number of components, and of each edge belonging to each component, taking into account the uncertainty in the edge weights.

Components are labelled in increasing order of their mean, so component 1 is always the weakest type of edge.

See also

get_network_component_probabilities(), get_edge_component_probabilities(), get_component_means(), plot_mixture()

Examples

sim_data <- simulate_bison_model_mixture(
  "binary", num_components = 2, component_weights = c(0.5, 0.5)
)
fit_edge <- bison_model(
  (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1_id, node_2_id),
  data = sim_data$df_sim,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)
fit_mixture <- bison_mixture(fit_edge, num_components = 3, verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit_mixture)
#> === Fitted dyadic mixture model ===
#> Maximum number of components: 3
#> Most probable number of components: 1
#> Posterior probability: 93.7%
#> === Component probabilities ===
#>            1     2     3
#> P(K=k) 0.937 0.056 0.007
#> === Component means (K = 1) ===
#>            1
#> median 0.439
#> === Edge component probabilities (K = 1) ===
#>         1
#> 1 <-> 2 1
#> 1 <-> 3 1
#> 1 <-> 4 1
#> 1 <-> 5 1
#> 1 <-> 6 1
#> 1 <-> 7 1
#> ... (99 more rows; see get_edge_component_probabilities())
